name: Aveteian
confidence_why: No source describes Aveteian stress directly: the only statement is an areal remark by Charpentier (1982a), quoted second-hand by Lynch and Crowley (2001), that the languages of central Malakula carry a strong penultimate accent, and Tryon (1976) supplies only a wordlist, so any penultimate reading for Aveteian is a guess by analogy with its neighbours.
catalog_citation: Lynch, John & Terry Crowley. 2001. Languages of Vanuatu: A new survey and bibliography. Pacific Linguistics 517. Canberra: ANU. p.71 fn.6 (quoting Charpentier, Jean-Michel. 1982a. Atlas linguistique du Sud-Malakula, vol. 1, p.63) and p.84 §3.7.25(2) Aveteian.
catalog_locator: p.71, footnote 6 in §3.7.1 Lendamboi; Aveteian entry p.84 §3.7.25(2)
catalog_quote: [p.71 fn.6] Charpentier (1982a:63) notes that in "the languages of the center of the island, there is a strong tonic accent on the next to last syllable, and the final vowel is so destressed as to become almost unrecognizeable [sic]", which accounts for the transcriptions with subscript vowel symbols. However, the phonemic status of these is not clearly indicated. ... [p.84 (2) Aveteian] Charpentier (1982a:45) indicates that, in the early twentieth century, a few families lived to the north of the Ninde-speaking area and spoke the separate language Aveteian, with a name that he represents phonetically as [avəteiana]. This language is possibly now extinct, and Charpentier (1982b) records nothing of it. Tryon (1976) includes a vocabulary gathered by G.J. Fox under the heading Dixon Reef 1. From its geographical source, this vocabulary may well represent Aveteian, especially as it is different to both of Charpentier's vocabularies for Nasarian and Letemboi, speakers of which currently live at Dixon Reef.

The footnote reads exactly as quoted: 'Charpentier (1982a:63) notes that in "the languages of the center of the island, there is a strong tonic accent on the next to last syllable, and the final vowel is so destressed as to become almost unrecognizeable [sic]", which accounts for the transcriptions with subscript vowel symbols. new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand areal generalisation: in the languages of the interior/centre of (south) Malakula there is a strong accent on the penultimate syllable and the final vowel is heavily reduced. Not stated for Dixon Reef/Aveteian specifically; whether Aveteian (spoken north of the Ninde area, west Malakula) falls under 'the center of the island' is not said.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Separately, Tryon 1976:47 (POC vowel correspondences, row 111 Dixon Reef) gives *u > ə 'In unstressed position' (fn.5), implying stressed/unstressed alternation in the Dixon Reef I data, but without saying where stress falls.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('next to last syllable'), from transcription practice in Charpentier's wordlists; areal statement covering the Lendamboi/Small Nambas interior languages, quoted by the survey in the Lendamboi section, not in the Aveteian entry. Lynch & Crowley add that the phonemic status of the reduced final vowels is unclear.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog dixo1238 'Dixon Reef' (ISO dix) = Aveteian (Charpentier 1982a:45 [avəteiana]; François et al. 2015 table row 101). 'Dixon Reef' (Tavendrua) is a coastal village where speakers of several interior languages now live; Tryon 1976's list 111 'Dixon Reef I' (G.J. Fox) is what Lynch & Crowley 2001:84 tentatively identify as Aveteian, while Tryon's 'Dixon Reef II (Ma)' (list 111a, Charpentier) is Nasarian [nvh], and the language currently used in Dixon Reef village is Lendamboi/Letemboi (Lynch & Crowley 2001:72). The quoted stress remark is an areal statement about 'the languages of the center of the island' (interior south Malakula), not about Aveteian in particular.

sources.note: Survey, no phonology of Dixon Reef/Aveteian. p.71 fn.6 (in §3.7.1 Lendamboi) quotes Charpentier 1982a:63: in 'the languages of the center of the island, there is a strong tonic accent on the next to last syllable, and the final vowel is so destressed as to become almost unrecognizeable' — an areal remark, not tied to Aveteian. §3.7.25(2) Aveteian p.84: possibly extinct; Charpentier 1982b records nothing of it; Tryon 1976 'Dixon Reef I' list (G.J. Fox) 'may well represent Aveteian'. §3.7.25(1) p.84: Tryon's 'Dixon Reef II' list = Nasarian.
